name: New Delhi
tagline: Mughal grandeur and leafy avenues at India's imperial capital.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Oct, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: October to March is the pleasant season, crowned by the Republic Day parade and Diwali; avoid the May-June furnace and January's smog and fog.

ourTake.lede: Delhi is two cities, the Mughal old town and the leafy colonial capital, and you need a day for each. Do Humayun's Tomb over the Red Fort if you have to choose; it's calmer and, many think, more beautiful. Go to Old Delhi early with a guide for the food and the Jama Masjid, and avoid the touts around the big monuments by having a driver and a plan.
ourTake.comeIf: You want Mughal monuments, layered history and the gateway to the Golden Triangle.
ourTake.skipIf: You want calm, clean air or a beach.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Andaz Delhi
credentials: MICHELIN Key, Selected (2025)
items.description: Design-led Hyatt Andaz minutes from the terminals, the sharpest of the airport-side luxury houses.

items.name: Taj Palace, New Delhi
items.area: Lutyens' / Central Delhi (Sardar Patel Marg, Diplomatic Enclave)
credentials: Houses Masala Art & Blue Ginger, Taj signature dining; Condé Nast Traveller India, recognised group
items.description: A vast garden-set Taj in the Diplomatic Enclave, built for scale, conferences and big Indian celebrations.

items.name: Qutub Minar & the Qutub Complex
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Qutub Minar and its Monuments
items.description: The 73-metre fluted victory tower of 1193 is the tallest brick minaret in the world, ringed by the ruins of India's first mosque and the uncorroded 4th-century Iron Pillar. Come at opening hour with a private ASI-trained guide before the coach crowds arrive; it is a short drive from the Mehrauli boutique hotels and the perfect first read of Delhi's layered history.

items.name: Humayun's Tomb
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Humayun's Tomb
items.description: The garden-tomb that rehearsed the Taj Mahal a century early, a red-sandstone and marble mausoleum floating in a formal charbagh, exquisitely restored by the Aga Khan Trust. Go in the low gold of late afternoon; it is the single most composed piece of Mughal architecture in the city and pairs naturally with an adjoining visit to Sunder Nursery and Nizamuddin.

items.name: Red Fort (Lal Qila)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Red Fort Complex
items.description: Shah Jahan's walled palace-city in red sandstone, from whose ramparts the Prime Minister addresses the nation each Independence Day. Walk the Diwan-i-Khas where the Peacock Throne once stood and the marble pavilions of the imperial harem; a good guide makes the faded splendour legible. Enter early to beat the heat and the queues at the Lahori Gate.

items.name: Jama Masjid
items.description: India's largest mosque, Shah Jahan's final architectural flourish, its red-and-white courtyard holding twenty-five thousand worshippers beneath three marble domes. Climb the southern minaret for the definitive rooftop view over Old Delhi's sea of terraces. Dress modestly, remove shoes, and time a visit to fold into a Chandni Chowk food walk next door.

items.name: Chandni Chowk
items.description: The 17th-century spine of Mughal Delhi, a delirium of jewellers, wedding-card printers, saree wholesalers and legendary food, laid out by Shah Jahan's daughter around a moonlit canal that is long gone. The civilised way to see it is a private morning walk or a cycle-rickshaw through the lanes, ending at Karim's or Paranthe Wali Gali; almost everything worth eating here is vegetarian-friendly.

items.name: Khari Baoli Spice Market
items.description: Asia's largest wholesale spice market, trading in cardamom, saffron, dried fruit and chilli from sack-piled shopfronts since the 17th century, the air itself makes you sneeze. Go with a guide who can walk you up to a rooftop godown for the panorama and translate the grading of the saffron and the pistachios, then buy a kilo of the good stuff to carry home.

items.name: Old Delhi Haveli Heritage Walk (Haveli Dharampura)
credentials: UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award of Merit for Cultural Heritage Conservation, Haveli Dharampura
items.description: A meticulously restored late-Mughal mansion in the Shahjahanabad lanes, brought back from ruin over six years and now an award-winning heritage hotel with kathak evenings in its sandstone courtyard. A guided haveli walk decodes the vanishing domestic architecture of Old Delhi, jharokha balconies, carved brackets, hidden courtyards, best ended over a rooftop dinner above the rooftops.

items.name: Lodhi Gardens
items.description: Ninety acres of landscaped calm scattered with the domed tombs of the 15th-century Sayyid and Lodhi sultans, Delhi's most beloved green room, where the city's elite walk their dogs at dawn. Come early for the birdsong and the light through the Bara Gumbad; it sits within a short walk of the Lodhi Hotel, Khan Market and the India International Centre.

items.name: India Gate & Kartavya Path
items.description: Lutyens' 42-metre war memorial arch anchoring the grand ceremonial vista of the redesigned Kartavya Path (formerly Rajpath), sweeping up to Rashtrapati Bhavan. The lawns come alive on winter evenings with families and ice-cream carts; drive the axis after dark when the whole processional way is floodlit, or stroll it at dusk from a Lutyens' Delhi hotel.

items.name: Rashtrapati Bhavan
items.description: Lutyens' colossal presidential palace, 340 rooms crowning Raisina Hill, a fusion of classical and Indian idioms that is arguably the grandest work of the Raj. Book ahead for the guided circuit of the state rooms and the Rashtrapati Bhavan Museum; the whole imperial city of New Delhi radiates from here, and it reads best with a historian at your side.

items.name: Amrit Udyan (the Mughal Gardens)
items.description: The formal terraced gardens behind Rashtrapati Bhavan, Persian charbagh geometry, a rose garden and a bonsai collection, thrown open to the public only in spring, when the tulips and the flowerbeds peak. Entry is free but slotted, from roughly February to March; book online, go on a weekday morning, and treat it as a seasonal event rather than a year-round stop.

items.name: Swaminarayan Akshardham
credentials: Guinness World Record, World's Largest Comprehensive Hindu Temple
items.description: A staggering pink-sandstone and marble temple carved by eleven thousand artisans without structural steel, ringed by a musical fountain, boat ride and manicured gardens on the Yamuna's east bank. Recognised by Guinness as the world's largest comprehensive Hindu temple. Allow half a day, note that phones and bags are barred inside, and know the vegetarian food court is genuinely good.

items.name: Lotus Temple (Bahá'í House of Worship)
items.description: Twenty-seven marble 'petals' folding into a serene lotus, one of the most-visited buildings on earth and a modern architectural landmark open to all faiths for silent meditation. Come near closing for the softest light on the white shell and the quietest hall; it sits a short hop from the Kalkaji temples and Nehru Place, and asks only stillness of its visitors.

items.name: Gurudwara Bangla Sahib
items.description: The most visited Sikh shrine in Delhi, its golden dome mirrored in a vast holy tank, with round-the-clock hymns and a langar kitchen that feeds tens of thousands free every day. Cover your head, walk through the sarovar, and if you can, step into the community kitchen to watch the sheer scale of the seva, it is one of the city's most moving sights, and entirely vegetarian.

items.name: Hazrat Nizamuddin Dargah
items.description: The 14th-century Sufi shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya, still the beating spiritual heart of a warren of medieval lanes, and on Thursday evenings the setting for live qawwali that has run in an unbroken tradition for centuries. Go with a knowledgeable guide, cover your head, and sit for the Thursday qawwali; the intensity of the devotion here is unlike anywhere else in Delhi.

items.name: Safdarjung's Tomb
items.description: The last great garden-tomb of the Mughals, built in 1754 in a slightly overblown late style that historians call the empire's 'last flicker', a domed marble mausoleum in a quiet charbagh that most visitors skip. That is exactly its charm: a serene, uncrowded stop minutes from Lodhi Gardens, ideal for a photographer or anyone who wants the Mughal aesthetic without the queues.

items.name: National Museum
items.description: India's premier collection, Harappan artefacts including the 4,500-year-old bronze Dancing Girl, Chola bronzes, Mughal miniatures, and relics of the Buddha. It is under long-term redevelopment, so check current access, but a private curator-led tour of the highlights gives the deepest single grounding in the subcontinent's art you can get in one building.

items.name: National Gallery of Modern Art
items.description: Housed in the former palace of the Maharaja of Jaipur near India Gate, this is the country's foremost collection of modern Indian art, Raja Ravi Varma, the Bengal School, Amrita Sher-Gil, the Progressives. A calm, well-lit couple of hours that maps the arc of Indian modernism, and an easy pairing with Bikaner House across the hexagon.

items.name: Sunder Nursery
credentials: Part of the Humayun's Tomb UNESCO World Heritage buffer; UNESCO Asia-Pacific Award-winning conservation by the Aga Khan Trust
items.description: A 90-acre 16th-century heritage park beside Humayun's Tomb, restored by the Aga Khan Trust into Delhi's first arboretum, with Mughal-era monuments, lily pools, a rose garden and over three hundred tree species. It is the most beautifully kept green space in the city, come for a slow morning, a picnic on the lawns, and the Sunday farmers' market when it runs.

items.name: National Crafts Museum (Crafts Museum)
items.description: A living museum of Indian folk and tribal craft, terracotta shrines, a full carved Gujarati haveli facade, textiles and votive art, with resident master artisans demonstrating and selling their work in the courtyards. It is a discreet, deeply rewarding stop for anyone who collects, and the on-site Café Lota is one of the best regional-Indian lunches in the city.

items.name: Hauz Khas Village & Lake
items.description: A 13th-century royal reservoir and the ruins of Firoz Shah's madrasa and tomb, wrapped by a deer park, and abutting an urban village of design boutiques, galleries and rooftop restaurants. Come late afternoon: the medieval monuments glow over the lake, then the lanes turn to shopping and cocktails. A rare place where deep history and contemporary Delhi sit side by side.

items.name: Dilli Haat (INA)
items.description: A permanent open-air crafts and food bazaar where artisans from every state rotate through the stalls, so you can buy Kashmiri pashmina, Channapatna toys or Odisha ikat direct from the maker without the tout-heavy chaos of a street market. Regional food stalls let you eat your way across India in an afternoon; good for gifts and for a relaxed, curated shop.

items.name: Khan Market
items.description: Reputedly among the most expensive retail streets in the world, this compact Lutyens' market is Delhi's most civilised shopping enclave, Good Earth and Anokhi for home and textiles, Full Circle bookshop, Fabindia, artisanal patisseries and quietly excellent restaurants above the shopfronts. The default afternoon for well-heeled Delhi, walkable from the Lodhi and Sujan hotels.

items.name: Mehrauli Archaeological Park
items.description: A sprawling, semi-wild park layering a thousand years of ruins, the Jamali-Kamali mosque and tomb, Balban's tomb, stepwells and Metcalfe's colonial folly, almost none of it ticketed or crowded. Go with a heritage guide and stout shoes; it is the connoisseur's counterpoint to the polished Qutub complex next door, best for a cool-season morning.

items.name: Agrasen ki Baoli
items.description: A dramatic 60-metre stepwell of 108 stone steps descending into shadow, hidden among the high-rises off Connaught Place, atmospheric, faintly eerie and beloved of photographers and film crews. A quick, striking stop between Lutyens' sights; go early before the Instagram crowd fills the steps, and let the sheer geometry of the descent do its work.

items.name: Bikaner House
items.description: The restored Delhi residence of the Maharaja of Bikaner at the India Gate hexagon, now a serious contemporary-arts venue hosting the city's best rotating gallery shows, design fairs and a satellite programme during India Art Fair week. Time a visit to whatever exhibition is up, then lunch at Chor Bizarre or L'Opéra on the premises; entry to the galleries is free.

items.name: Kiran Nadar Museum of Art (KNMA)
items.description: India's leading private art museum, holding one of the finest collections of modern and contemporary Indian art, Husain, Gaitonde, Sher-Gil and a strong contemporary program, with free entry and ambitious curation. A polished, air-conditioned hour or two for serious art-lovers; a landmark new building near the airport is in the works, so the Saket galleries are the current home.

items.name: Chhatarpur Temple (Shri Adya Katyayani Shakti Peeth)
items.description: One of India's largest temple complexes, a sprawling white confection of carved marble and pink sandstone shrines set in gardens on Delhi's southern edge, thronged especially during Navratri. It is a study in the exuberance of modern Hindu temple-building rather than antiquity, a striking, uncrowded-by-tourist stop en route to or from the Qutub and Mehrauli.

items.name: Purana Qila (Old Fort)
items.description: The massive walls of the sixteenth-century citadel of Sher Shah Suri and Humayun, said to sit on the legendary site of Indraprastha of the Mahabharata, with a graceful mosque, an octagonal library tower, and archaeological digs that keep pushing Delhi's history deeper. Quiet, monumental, and beside the Delhi Zoo; go early and let the ramparts and the boating lake set the mood.

items.name: Jantar Mantar
items.description: Maharaja Jai Singh II's masterful astronomical instruments of 1724, giant masonry sundials and celestial dials built to chart the heavens with the naked eye, standing in a garden minutes from Connaught Place. A short, cerebral stop that rewards a guide who can explain how each surreal red structure actually measures time and the stars.

items.name: Gandhi Smriti (Birla House)
items.description: The house where Mahatma Gandhi spent his last 144 days and was assassinated in 1948, preserved as a moving memorial with his spartan room left as it was and his final footsteps marked across the garden. A quiet, essential half-hour of modern Indian history, close to the Lutyens' hotels and often paired with the National Gandhi Museum near Raj Ghat.

items.name: Raj Ghat
items.description: The riverside memorial marking Gandhi's cremation, a simple black marble platform, an eternal flame and a lawn where visiting heads of state come to lay wreaths. Understated and contemplative; slip your shoes off, and pair it with the nearby memorials to India's other prime ministers along the Yamuna if the mood is reflective.

items.name: Old Delhi Food Walk
items.description: A guided crawl through the alleys around Chandni Chowk and Jama Masjid, Mughlai kebabs and nihari, jalebis fried in ghee, kachoris, kulfi and Karim's, is the tastiest single day in Delhi. Book a reputable private walk that curates the hygienic legends; vegetarian and Jain-friendly itineraries are easy to arrange, from Paranthe Wali Gali to the sweet shops of Ghantewala's heirs.

items.name: Nizamuddin & Nizamuddin East Walk
items.description: A single walkable knot holds the Dargah, the tomb of the poet Amir Khusrau, Ghalib's memorial, Chausath Khamba and the exquisite Barapula-era monuments, seven centuries of Sufi Delhi in a few hundred metres. The Aga Khan Trust's neighbourhood renewal has made it navigable; a specialist guide turns the tangle into one of the richest heritage walks in India.

items.name: Jama Masjid to Feroz Shah Kotla
items.description: The ruined fourteenth-century citadel of Feroz Shah Tughlaq, crowned by a polished Ashokan pillar the sultan hauled from Ambala and re-erected, and famous today for the crowds who leave letters to the djinns in its cellars every Thursday. An offbeat, atmospheric ruin for those who have done the headline forts and want the stranger Delhi.

items.name: Sulabh International Museum of Toilets
items.description: One of the world's genuinely unusual museums, tracing 4,500 years of sanitation from Harappan drains to ornate Victorian commodes, quirky, oddly fascinating, and regularly listed among the strangest museums on earth. A short, memorable detour with children or the incurably curious; not everyone's stop, but nobody forgets it.

items.name: Garden of Five Senses
items.description: A twenty-acre landscaped park near Mehrauli threaded with sculpture, themed gardens, terraced rockeries and an evening food-and-shopping plaza, designed for wandering rather than monument-ticking. A relaxed sunset stroll, popular with Delhi families, and an easy add-on when you are already out at the Qutub or Chhatarpur.

items.name: Sarojini Nagar & Janpath Markets
items.description: The city's great bargain bazaars, Sarojini for export-surplus fashion at a fraction of retail, Janpath for Rajasthani textiles, silver and trinkets. Not luxury, but a gleefully local thing to do: send an assistant or go with a savvy friend, haggle hard, and come away with a bag of finds. A fun counterweight to a Khan Market afternoon.

items.name: Kingsway Camp & Coronation Park
items.description: The forlorn field where the 1911 Delhi Durbar crowned George V, now a haunting open-air graveyard of exiled Raj statues, a colossal George V, viceroys and generals, banished from the city centre after Independence. Utterly offbeat and a little melancholy; a stop for history obsessives and photographers rather than the casual visitor.

items.name: Taj Mahal & Agra Day Trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Taj Mahal; UNESCO, Agra Fort
items.description: The obvious and unimpeachable day trip: Shah Jahan's marble tomb to Mumtaz Mahal, plus Agra Fort and the jewel-like 'Baby Taj', roughly three hours down the Yamuna Expressway or under two by the Gatimaan Express. Do it with a private car and guide, start before dawn for the Taj at sunrise, and consider a night at the Oberoi Amarvilas with its every-room Taj view rather than rushing back.

items.name: Neemrana Fort-Palace Day Trip
items.description: A restored 15th-century Aravalli hill-fort turned India's first heritage hotel, about two hours from Delhi on the Jaipur road, terraced ramparts, hanging gardens, a spa and a Flying Fox zipline off the battlements. A civilised lunch-and-walk day, or a serene overnight to break the Delhi–Jaipur drive; non-residents can book the palace lunch and tour.

items.name: Mathura & Vrindavan Day Trip
items.description: The birthplace of Krishna and the town of his youth, a cluster of thousands of temples and ghats about three to four hours south of Delhi, most intense during the Holi celebrations, which are legendary here. A private car and a temple-savvy guide make the crowds manageable; go for the living devotion, the Banke Bihari temple and the evening aarti on the Yamuna.

items.name: Sultanpur National Park & Bird Sanctuary
items.description: A compact wetland reserve about an hour from central Delhi that draws migratory flamingos, pelicans, storks and hundreds of species through the winter months. An easy, gentle morning with binoculars and a naturalist for birders and multi-generational groups wanting green quiet near the city; best from November to March.

items.name: Cycle Tour of New Delhi at Dawn
items.description: Before the city wakes, a guided cycle through the empty avenues of Lutyens' Delhi and the sleeping lanes of Old Delhi, past Rashtrapati Bhavan, the war memorial and the wholesale bazaars stirring to life, is the most magical way to feel the two Delhis. Operators provide good bikes and small groups; the cool air and empty roads make it worth the early alarm.

items.name: Olive Bar & Kitchen
credentials: Condé Nast Traveller India Top Restaurant Awards 2024, No. 6

items.description: A spirited take on regional Indian street and home cooking, bold, affordable and genuinely fun.

items.name: Karim's
credentials: Time Out Delhi, landmark Old Delhi institution
110+ years; recognised heritage restaurant of the capital
items.description: Since 1913, the definitive Old Delhi Mughlai kitchen, from a family that once cooked for the last Mughal court.

items.name: 1911 Bar
credentials: Inside The Imperial, MICHELIN Two Keys (2025)
items.description: The colonnaded colonial-era bar at The Imperial, rare whiskies beneath 1930s Lutyens grandeur.

items.name: Lair

Rakshay Dhariwal's original Delhi speakeasy
items.description: The faux phone-booth speakeasy that started Delhi's hidden-bar movement in 2012, still one of its most stylish rooms.

items.area: Lutyens' / Central Delhi (The Oberoi, New Delhi)
credentials: Inside The Oberoi, New Delhi, MICHELIN One Key (2025)
items.description: The Oberoi's rooftop bar, city-light views, careful cocktails and the calm precision of the house.

plan.heading: 3 days in New Delhi, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Check into The Oberoi, New Delhi, overlooking the golf course and Humayun's Tomb.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Private visit to Humayun's Tomb and the restored Sunder Nursery gardens beside it.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Indian Accent at The Lodhi, Manish Mehrotra's inventive Indian tasting menu.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Early walk through Shahjahanabad, Jama Masjid, the spice lanes of Khari Baoli, a cycle-rickshaw through Chandni Chowk.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Rest, then Qutub Minar and the Mehrauli Archaeological Park in the softer afternoon light.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dine at Bukhara at ITC Maurya, the North-West Frontier grill room that has fed heads of state.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The National Museum, or the private Kiran Nadar collection of modern Indian art.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lodhi Gardens on foot, then tea and shopping for textiles at Good Earth and the design stores of Meharchand Market.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A last dinner at Avartana or a quiet evening at The Oberoi's Threesixty before departure.

items.name: Lutyens' / Central Delhi
items.description: Broad green avenues and the grand hotels, calm and well-connected.

items.name: Old Delhi (Shahjahanabad)
items.description: The Mughal walled city of lanes and mosques, intense and unmissable by day.

items.name: South Delhi (Hauz Khas / Mehrauli)
items.description: Village ruins, boutiques and restaurants, for a younger, greener stay.

events.name: Republic Day parade
events.note: The nation's grand military and cultural parade down Kartavya Path.

events.name: Diwali
events.note: The festival of lights transforms the city with lamps and fireworks; date follows the lunar calendar.

events.name: Qutub / India Art Fair season
events.note: India's leading art fair draws collectors, alongside heritage festivals in the cooler months.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Stay in Lutyens' Delhi (Aman, The Oberoi, The Imperial) for calm and proximity; air quality dips sharply October to January, so plan indoor mornings then.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Arrive at Indira Gandhi International Airport (DEL) Terminal 3, where a chauffeured car and, on request, fast-track immigration meet you at the aerobridge.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car with driver is essential across Delhi's distances; the metro is efficient but not how a UHNI traveller moves here.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Excellent 5G and hotel wifi; an Indian eSIM or Airtel/Jio SIM is simple, though most arrivals rely on their concierge's device.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The Indian rupee (INR); cards work everywhere formal, keep cash for markets and drivers, and tipping around ten percent is customary.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Oct-Mar is the kind window, crisp and clear for the monuments; Nov-Jan can bring heavy morning fog and hazardous air. Avoid Apr-Jun, when heat pushes past 40C, and the Jul-Sep monsoon humidity.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Home hub: Indira Gandhi International (DEL) is a primary origin, so no connection needed from Delhi and a short 2-2.5 hour hop from Mumbai or Bengaluru on Vistara or IndiGo. Terminal 3 is the premium terminal; use the Air India or Plaza Premium lounges, and pre-arrange chauffeur pickup to skip the arrivals crush.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: Routine vaccines plus Hepatitis A and typhoid advised; drink only sealed or filtered water. Delhi is generally safe in the central and diplomatic areas with sensible discretion; the genuine concern is winter air quality (Nov-Jan), which can be severe for anyone sensitive.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Effortless for vegetarian and Jain travellers; most fine kitchens keep dedicated Jain preparations. This is Indian food at its source, from Bukhara and Dum Pukht to Indian Accent for a modern vegetarian tasting menu.
